impacts.caseName: Teva Pharmaceuticals International GmbH v. Eli Lilly and Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in granting judgment as a matter of law that Teva's headache patents claiming methods of using humanized anti-CGRP antagonist antibodies to treat headache were invalid for failure to satisfy the written-description and enablement requirements of 35 U.S.C. § 112.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's JMOL invalidating Teva's headache patents under § 112, after a jury had found willful infringement by Lilly and rejected invalidity. The case involves Teva's Ajovy product and Lilly's competing anti-CGRP antibody treatment, with significant implications for the scope of patent claims covering biologic drug classes.
impacts.positiveImplications: Strengthens the ability of pharmaceutical and biotech companies to obtain and enforce genus claims covering classes of biologics (e.g., humanized antibodies) based on disclosure of one species and known methods of making others, protecting broader patent portfolios.
impacts.negativeImplications: Generic and biosimilar competitors face greater risk that broad genus claims in biologics patents will survive validity challenges, potentially extending periods of market exclusivity.

impacts.caseName: A.L.M. Holding Company v. Zydex Industries Private Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a patent owner that licenses exclusive commercialization rights but retains the right to sue for infringement (not rendered illusory) has sufficient constitutional standing to bring an infringement action.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed dismissal for lack of standing, holding that a patent owner retaining a non-illusory right to sue third parties for infringement—even after granting an exclusive license to commercialize—satisfies Article III standing. The court analyzed the retained exclusionary rights under the licensing agreement.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent owners structuring license agreements can retain standing to enforce patents by preserving meaningful exclusionary rights, providing flexibility in licensing while maintaining enforcement capability.
impacts.negativeImplications: Accused infringers may face suits from patent holders who have already licensed away most commercial rights, complicating settlement dynamics and potentially increasing the volume of patent litigation.

impacts.caseName: Ollnova Technologies Ltd. v. Ecobee Technologies ULC
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in using a single jury verdict question covering infringement of all asserted patents and in its application of the Alice two-step framework for patent eligibility under 35 U.S.C. § 101 for patents directed to wireless building automation systems.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the $11.5 million infringement and damages judgments and remanded for a new trial, finding that the single-question verdict form covering all asserted patents was prejudicial error. The court also vacated and remanded the § 101 analysis for the '495 patent while affirming eligibility for other patents.
impacts.positiveImplications: Reinforces that patents directed to specific technical improvements in wireless building automation systems (rather than abstract ideas) can survive § 101 challenges, supporting IoT and smart-device patent holders.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders must ensure verdict forms separately address infringement for each asserted patent; failure to do so risks vacatur of multi-million dollar judgments, increasing litigation costs on retrial.

impacts.caseName: Ironburg Inventions Ltd. v. Valve Corporation
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court properly applied IPR estoppel under 35 U.S.C. § 315(e)(2) to bar Valve from asserting invalidity grounds not raised in its prior IPR petition, and whether hindsight bias was adequately considered in that analysis.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's application of IPR estoppel against Valve on two invalidity grounds, finding insufficient evidence to support estoppel on one ground and failure to account for hindsight bias on the other. The decision narrows the scope of estoppel applied to IPR petitioners in subsequent district court litigation.
impacts.positiveImplications: Companies defending against patent infringement retain broader ability to assert invalidity defenses in district court even after filing IPR petitions, as courts must carefully evaluate whether prior art reasonably could have been discovered without hindsight.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face weakened estoppel protections from IPR proceedings, meaning defendants may raise additional invalidity arguments in district court that they did not include in their IPR petitions.

impacts.caseName: Insulet Corp. v. EOFlow, Co. Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the statute of limitations under the Defend Trade Secrets Act (DTSA) had expired before Insulet brought suit, where the alleged misappropriation of trade secrets related to insulin pump technology occurred in 2018 and suit was filed in August 2023.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's denial of JMOL and found that EOFlow was entitled to judgment as a matter of law because the DTSA's three-year statute of limitations had expired before Insulet filed suit. The court concluded Insulet knew or should have known of the misappropriation more than three years before filing.
impacts.positiveImplications: Companies accused of trade secret misappropriation benefit from strict enforcement of the DTSA's three-year limitations period, providing certainty and finality against stale claims.
impacts.negativeImplications: Trade secret holders must act promptly upon discovering or having reason to discover misappropriation; delayed investigation or litigation strategy risks losing the ability to pursue DTSA claims entirely, even where misappropriation is proven.

impacts.caseName: Versata Software, LLC v. Ford Motor Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in excluding Versata's trade secret damages expert and in its judgment on damages for trade secret misappropriation and breach of contract arising from Ford's development of competing manufacturing configuration software.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the trade secret damages judgment and remanded for a new trial, instructing the district court to reconsider two previously rejected damages models. The court also reversed the district court's reduction of the breach of contract jury award and reinstated it. The court affirmed Ford's liability for trade secret misappropriation under both the DTSA and Michigan law.
impacts.positiveImplications: Software licensors benefit from expanded damages theories in trade secret cases and protection of jury awards for breach of contract claims, reinforcing the value of proprietary software and licensing agreements.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies that develop competing products after licensing third-party software face significant trade secret misappropriation liability and may face retrial on expanded damages theories, increasing litigation exposure.

impacts.caseName: International Medical Devices, Inc. v. Cornell
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the jury's finding that plaintiffs had met their burden to show each asserted trade secret was protectable under California law was supported by legally sufficient evidence, and whether an inventor's contribution of generally known ideas can establish patent inventorship.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the denial of JMOL on trade secret claims, holding there was insufficient evidence that the asserted trade secrets were protectable under California law because the information was generally known. The court also reversed on patent invalidity, finding that contributions of generally known ideas cannot constitute inventive contributions for inventorship purposes. The counterfeiting claim and damages were affirmed.
impacts.positiveImplications: Defendants in trade secret cases benefit from rigorous evidentiary scrutiny of whether asserted information qualifies as protectable; companies cannot claim trade secret protection over generally known information even where confidentiality agreements exist.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies relying on trade secret claims to protect business methods or product designs face higher evidentiary burdens to demonstrate information is not generally known in the industry, potentially weakening IP enforcement strategies.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a corporate Rule 30(b)(6) designee may testify at summary judgment regarding facts outside the designee's personal knowledge, and whether computer source code constitutes hearsay.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed summary judgment of patent invalidity under the on-sale bar, holding that a 30(b)(6) corporate representative may testify about matters outside personal knowledge at summary judgment, and that computer source code (as opposed to human-authored descriptions within code) is not hearsay. The prior art device's commercial sales before the critical date invalidated the patent.
impacts.positiveImplications: Companies defending against patents can use 30(b)(6) witnesses to establish prior art sales even when no engineer with personal knowledge is available, and can rely on source code as non-hearsay evidence of functionality.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face broader evidentiary challenges at summary judgment, as corporate representatives without personal knowledge can testify about historical products and source code evidence is more readily admissible to prove on-sale bar invalidity.

impacts.caseName: VLSI Technology LLC v. Intel Corporation
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court correctly granted summary judgment of noninfringement based on extraterritoriality and the doctrine of equivalents for patents relating to multi-core processor task selection.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit partially reversed summary judgment of noninfringement of the '836 patent, addressing the extraterritorial reach of U.S. patent law in the context of semiconductor chip manufacturing and design occurring partly overseas. The court also addressed the striking of damages expert theories for inadequate disclosure.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders asserting infringement of semiconductor and processor patents may have broader reach where accused activities have a sufficient domestic nexus, reversing an overly narrow application of extraterritoriality limits.
impacts.negativeImplications: Semiconductor companies with global manufacturing and design operations face increased patent infringement exposure in the U.S. even for activities partially conducted abroad.

impacts.caseName: Enanta Pharmaceuticals, Inc. v. Pfizer Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the '953 patent could claim priority from a provisional application where the provisional contained 'C2-C12-alkyl' and the issued patent changed it to 'C1-C12-alkyl,' allegedly correcting a typographical error, and whether Pfizer's intervening disclosure of nirmatrelvir anticipated the claims.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed summary judgment invalidating Enanta's patent covering compounds used to inhibit coronavirus replication, finding that the change from C2 to C1 in the substituent definition was not an obvious typographical error correctable on its face. Because the patent could not claim priority from the provisional application, Pfizer's intervening public disclosure of nirmatrelvir (Paxlovid's active ingredient) anticipated the claims.
impacts.positiveImplications: Pharmaceutical companies benefit from certainty that competitors cannot retroactively expand provisional application disclosures through alleged typographical error corrections to capture subsequently disclosed compounds like nirmatrelvir.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent applicants face strict consequences for errors in provisional applications; even minor typographical mistakes in chemical formulas can destroy priority claims and render patents invalid when intervening prior art emerges.

impacts.caseName: Constellation Designs, LLC v. LG Electronics Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patents claiming non-uniform constellations for digital communication systems are patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether the district court's damages analysis and infringement findings were legally sufficient.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated eligibility for some claims while affirming eligibility for others, affirmed non-infringement and damages findings including the admissibility of damages expert testimony. The case provides significant guidance on the Alice framework for communications technology patents involving mathematical optimization of signal constellations.
impacts.positiveImplications: Communications technology patent holders receive guidance that claims tied to specific technical implementations (rather than abstract mathematical optimization) can survive § 101 challenges, supporting patent portfolios in wireless and broadcasting standards.
impacts.negativeImplications: Technology companies implementing communication standards face ongoing patent infringement risk where standard-essential patents survive eligibility challenges, potentially increasing licensing costs.

impacts.caseName: AGI SureTrack LLC v. Farmers Edge Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patents claiming automated systems for capturing, processing, and sharing farming data using passive data collection devices on farming equipment are directed to patent-ineligible abstract ideas under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether the case was exceptional warranting attorney fees.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed that AGI's asserted farming data collection patent claims were patent-ineligible under § 101 as directed to abstract ideas, but vacated and remanded on the exceptionality determination, suggesting the case may warrant attorney fees. The decision reinforces that data collection and processing claims in the agricultural technology space face significant § 101 hurdles.
impacts.positiveImplications: AgTech companies accused of infringement benefit from strong § 101 defense against broad data-collection claims, and the remand on exceptionality signals potential for fee-shifting against weak patent assertions.
impacts.negativeImplications: Agricultural technology patent holders face heightened § 101 invalidity risk for claims directed to automated farming data collection and processing, potentially undermining patent portfolios in the precision agriculture sector.

impacts.caseName: Actelion Pharmaceuticals Ltd v. Mylan Pharmaceuticals Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the claim term 'a pH of 13 or higher' in pharmaceutical composition patents refers to pH measured at a standard temperature in the field, and whether Actelion was barred from asserting infringement under the doctrine of equivalents.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed a finding of no literal infringement and no infringement by equivalents of Actelion's epoprostenol formulation patents against Mylan's generic drug, holding that pH claim terms must be interpreted at the temperature standard recognized in the field. The decision has implications for ANDA litigation involving pharmaceutical formulation claims with pH-dependent limitations.
impacts.positiveImplications: Generic pharmaceutical companies benefit from clear guidance that pH-related claim limitations are interpreted at recognized field standards, facilitating ANDA filings and generic drug approvals for pH-sensitive formulations.
impacts.negativeImplications: Brand pharmaceutical companies with formulation patents containing pH limitations may find their claims narrower than intended if pH measurements vary with temperature, potentially reducing patent protection for drug products.

impacts.caseName: Federal Express Corporation v. Qualcomm Incorporated
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a non-party to underlying patent litigation can file an IPR petition on the statutory deadline of a party to that litigation, effectively acting as a proxy to circumvent the time bar of 35 U.S.C. § 315(b), and whether the Board's obviousness determination was supported by substantial evidence.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the Board's obviousness determination invalidating FedEx's sensor-based logistics patent and remanded for further proceedings. The case raised significant concerns about third parties filing IPR petitions as proxies for time-barred litigants, though the court declined to review the Board's denial of FedEx's termination motion on that issue.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent owners benefit from the vacatur of an obviousness finding and the court's scrutiny of potential proxy IPR filings, which could deter abuse of the IPR system by third parties acting on behalf of time-barred defendants.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies relying on IPR petitions filed by third parties to challenge patents face uncertainty about the sustainability of those proceedings, particularly where the timing suggests coordination with time-barred litigation parties.

impacts.caseName: Fortress Iron, LP v. Digger Specialties, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a patent holder can correct inventorship under 35 U.S.C. § 256(b) through court action when an omitted co-inventor cannot be located, and whether the patents are invalid for incorrect inventorship when correction has not been completed.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed that the patents were invalid for omission of a co-inventor (a Chinese manufacturer's employee) where the patent holder could not locate the omitted inventor and thus could not complete correction. The court upheld the denial of the § 256(b) correction motion, leaving the patents invalid.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies collaborating with foreign manufacturers on product development face significant patent validity risk if foreign contributors qualify as co-inventors but cannot later be located for inventorship correction, potentially invalidating entire patent portfolios.
